q: Under the first method of lending recommended by the Tandon Committee, the maximum permissible bank finance is 75 per cent of the working capital gap, that is, current assets minus current liabilities other than bank borrowings. An enterprise has current assets of Rs 36,00,000 and such other current liabilities of Rs 12,00,000. Its maximum permissible bank finance under this method is:
The Chore Committee on the cash credit system recommended, among other things, that:

options.A: The borrower should be given a single undifferentiated cash credit limit for the whole year, with no review of its utilisation
options.B: Separate limits should be fixed for the peak season and the non-peak (normal) season, and the borrower should furnish quarterly statements of expected receipts and payments against the sanctioned limits
options.C: Banks should stop taking stock statements from borrowers enjoying working capital limits
options.D: The entire working capital requirement of a borrower should be met from long-term sources only

q: Working capital is estimated by the projected balance sheet method by:

options.A: Taking a fixed percentage of the projected sales of the coming year, without preparing any statement
options.B: Dividing the annual operating cost by the number of operating cycles in the year
options.C: Applying the current ratio of the previous year to the previous year's current liabilities
options.D: Preparing a forecast balance sheet for a future date, in which the projected current assets minus the projected current liabilities (other than the bank borrowing to be ascertained) give the working capital gap to be financed

q: An enterprise has permanent current assets of Rs 15,00,000 throughout the year and temporary current assets rising to Rs 6,00,000 at the seasonal peak. Following the matching (hedging) approach strictly, it should finance:

options.A: The whole Rs 21,00,000 from short-term sources, renewing them as they fall due
options.B: The permanent current assets of Rs 15,00,000 from long-term sources and the temporary current assets of Rs 6,00,000 from short-term sources
options.C: The whole Rs 21,00,000 from long-term sources, keeping the seasonal part idle in the slack season
options.D: The permanent current assets from short-term sources and the temporary current assets from long-term sources

q: Compared with an aggressive working capital financing policy, a conservative policy generally results in:

options.A: Lower liquidity and higher profitability, because long-term funds are costlier and are used sparingly
options.B: Higher risk of being unable to renew short-term borrowings on maturity
options.C: Higher liquidity and lower profitability, because costlier long-term funds are used even for seasonal needs and surplus funds remain idle in the slack season
options.D: No difference at all in either liquidity or profitability

q: In estimating the working capital of a manufacturing enterprise, debtors are commonly valued at the cost of sales rather than at the selling price, because:

options.A: The profit element in the selling price is not a fund actually blocked in the debtors; only the cost incurred has to be financed until collection
options.B: The selling price of the goods is never known in advance
options.C: Debtors are not a current asset at all
options.D: Credit sales are always made at a loss

q: A factory has 10,000 units in work-in-progress. Material costing Rs 40 per unit has been fully introduced, while labour of Rs 20 per unit and overheads of Rs 10 per unit (at full completion) are only 50 per cent complete on these units. The value of the work-in-progress to be taken in the working capital estimate is:

The annual demand for a material is 18,000 units, its Economic Order Quantity is 600 units, the ordering cost is Rs 50 per order and the carrying cost is Rs 5 per unit per year. At the Economic Order Quantity, the total annual ordering cost plus carrying cost is:
The annual demand for a component is 24,000 units and its Economic Order Quantity is 800 units. The number of orders to be placed during the year is:

options.A: 30 orders
options.B: 24 orders
options.C: 20 orders
options.D: 40 orders

q: The annual demand for a material is 36,000 units and its Economic Order Quantity is 1,200 units, reckoning a year of 360 days. The time interval between two successive orders is:

options.A: 10 days
options.B: 30 days
options.C: 12 days
options.D: 15 days

q: An enterprise proposes to extend its credit period. The extension is expected to raise sales by Rs 10,00,000, on which the contribution margin is 20 per cent. The net benefit of the proposal is:

options.A: 12.1 per cent
options.B: 32.3 per cent
options.C: 24.3 per cent
options.D: 3.1 per cent

q: Factoring of receivables differs from ordinary bill discounting mainly in that the factor, besides financing the receivables, also:

options.A: Undertakes services such as sales-ledger administration and collection of the debts, and in non-recourse factoring bears the loss from bad debts
options.B: Lends only against the security of immovable property of the enterprise
options.C: Requires the enterprise to repay the advance even before the customer pays, in every type of factoring
options.D: Is confined to the discounting of bills of exchange drawn on the government alone

q: A lock-box system is adopted by an enterprise for collecting its receivables primarily in order to:

options.A: Increase the credit period allowed to its customers
options.B: Postpone payment to its own suppliers for a longer period
options.C: Avoid maintaining any bank account for collections
options.D: Reduce the collection (mail and processing) float, by having customers remit to local post-office boxes from where the bank collects and credits the proceeds quickly

q: Trade credit and accrued wages and expenses are described as spontaneous sources of working capital finance because they:

options.A: Are available only after a formal loan agreement with a bank is executed
options.B: Carry the highest rate of interest among all sources of finance
options.C: Arise automatically, in the ordinary course of business, roughly in step with the level of operations, without a separate financing decision
options.D: Are raised from the shareholders of the enterprise

q: An enterprise disburses Rs 2,00,000 per day. By changing its disbursement arrangements it increases its disbursement float by 3 days, without delaying any payment beyond its due date. The amount of funds so released for use is:

options.A: 30 conversions
options.B: 18 conversions
options.C: 60 conversions
options.D: 12 conversions

q: Which of the following is a spontaneous source of working capital finance?

options.A: A term loan raised from a financial institution
options.B: A fresh issue of equity shares
options.C: Credit allowed by suppliers of raw material in the ordinary course of purchases
options.D: A debenture issue made to the public

q: Commercial paper, as a source of short-term finance for working capital, can be issued only by:

options.A: Any partnership firm, however small, without any condition
options.B: Creditworthy companies satisfying the prescribed eligibility conditions such as minimum net worth and a credit rating, for raising funds directly from investors for a short maturity
options.C: Enterprises which have defaulted on their bank borrowings
options.D: Co-operative societies alone

q: An enterprise whose sales are expanding very fast shows a falling current ratio, lengthening overdrafts and increasing dependence on supplier credit, even though it reports profits. These are typical symptoms of:

options.A: Under-trading, that is, carrying far more working capital than its operations need
options.B: A permanent surplus of long-term funds in the business
options.C: Complete absence of any credit sales
options.D: Over-trading, that is, expanding operations beyond what its working capital can support

q: Working capital leverage refers to the effect on the return on capital employed when:

options.A: The investment in current assets is reduced while sales and operating profit are maintained, so that the same profit is earned on a smaller capital base, though with greater liquidity risk
options.B: The proportion of debt in the capital structure is increased, whatever happens to current assets
options.C: Fixed assets are replaced by current assets of the same value
options.D: The credit period allowed to customers is lengthened without any change in sales

q: The daily operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 25,000. Its operating cycle lengthens by 10 days, other things remaining the same. The additional working capital it will require is:

The projected sales of an enterprise for the coming year are Rs 84,00,000 and, on the percentage-of-sales method, its working capital is estimated at 15 per cent of sales. The working capital required by the enterprise is:

The working capital of an enterprise is estimated from the following components: raw material stock Rs 2,40,000, work-in-progress Rs 1,20,000, finished goods stock Rs 3,00,000, debtors Rs 4,20,000 and cash Rs 60,000; against these, trade creditors are Rs 1,80,000 and outstanding wages are Rs 40,000. The net working capital required is:
The net working capital of an enterprise is estimated at Rs 12,50,000. A margin of 8 per cent is added for contingencies. The total working capital to be provided for is:

A cold-storage enterprise needs heavy funds for a few months of the year to buy and store the seasonal produce, while for the rest of the year its requirement is small and steady. The heavy seasonal requirement is an example of:

options.A: Fluctuating (temporary) working capital, over and above the permanent minimum level maintained throughout the year
options.B: Permanent (core) working capital, because it recurs every year
options.C: Fixed capital, because the produce is stored in its own building
options.D: Gross working capital of the enterprise as a whole

q: VED analysis, used for the control of spare-parts inventory, classifies items as Vital, Essential and Desirable primarily on the basis of:

options.A: The annual consumption value of the items
options.B: The criticality of the item for production, that is, the seriousness of the stoppage or loss caused if the item is not available when needed
options.C: The physical size and weight of the items
options.D: The speed with which the items move out of the stores

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 18,25,000 and its average inventory during the year is Rs 2,50,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. The number of days for which inventory is held, on an average, is:

options.A: 7.3 days
options.B: 73 days
options.C: 36.5 days
options.D: 50 days

q: The debtors of an enterprise stand at Rs 4,00,000 and its annual credit sales are Rs 36,50,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. Its average collection period is:

options.A: 30 days
options.B: 36.5 days
options.C: 40 days
options.D: 45 days

q: A division keeps its profit unchanged but increases the sales generated from the same capital employed. In Du Pont terms, the resulting rise in its Return on Investment comes through an improvement in:

options.A: The profit margin on sales alone
options.B: The capital turnover ratio
options.C: The capital charge rate
options.D: The residual income of the division

q: A division earns a controllable profit of Rs 5,40,000 on capital employed of Rs 36,00,000. Its Return on Investment is:

options.A: Residual Income rises whenever a project earns more than the capital charge on the investment it requires
options.B: Residual Income is expressed as a percentage and therefore always rises with new investment
options.C: Residual Income ignores the capital employed in the division altogether
options.D: Residual Income is computed before charging any cost of capital

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 3,10,000 on capital employed of Rs 31,00,000. The required rate of return is 12 per cent. Its Residual Income is:

options.B: Nil

q: Economic Value Added is best described as the value created in a period after meeting:

options.A: Only the interest payable to lenders
options.B: The cost of all capital employed, both debt and equity, applied to the net operating profit after tax
options.C: Only the dividend expected by equity shareholders
options.D: The depreciation charge on the assets employed

q: The Net Operating Profit After Tax of a division is Rs 9,60,000, its capital employed is Rs 60,00,000 and the weighted average cost of capital is 11 per cent. Its Economic Value Added is:

A division disposes of a long-idle asset that was earning nothing, its operating profit remaining the same and the sale proceeds being returned to head office. Other things equal, the disposal will improve its Economic Value Added mainly because:

options.A: Its sales turnover necessarily rises
options.B: Its tax charge for the year falls to nil
options.C: The capital on which the capital charge is levied becomes smaller
options.D: Its weighted average cost of capital becomes zero

q: A supplying division is working at full capacity and must turn away outside customers to meet an internal order. For goal congruence, the minimum transfer price it should charge must cover:

options.A: Its fixed cost per unit only
options.B: The historical cost recorded in its books
options.C: Only the depreciation on the plant used
options.D: Its variable cost per unit plus the contribution lost on the outside sales displaced

q: A supplying division has a variable cost of Rs 82 per unit. It works at full capacity and loses a contribution of Rs 28 per unit on outside sales for every unit transferred internally. The minimum transfer price per unit it should accept is:

options.A: Rs 82
options.B: Rs 110
options.C: Rs 54
options.D: Rs 138

q: The full cost of a component in the supplying division is Rs 240 per unit. Transfers are priced at full cost plus a mark-up of 25 per cent on cost. The transfer price per unit is:

options.A: Rs 265
options.B: Rs 288
options.C: Rs 300
options.D: Rs 320

q: The outside market price of an intermediate product is Rs 175 per unit. On an internal transfer, selling and distribution expenses of Rs 10 per unit that are incurred on outside sales are saved. The adjusted market-based transfer price per unit is:

options.A: Rs 165
options.B: Rs 175
options.C: Rs 185
options.D: Rs 160

q: Negotiated transfer prices can work satisfactorily only where:

options.A: Head office fixes both the price and the quantity in every case
options.B: The buying division is compelled to buy internally at any price named
options.C: The supplying division has no knowledge of its own costs
options.D: Both divisions enjoy autonomy, have access to cost and market information, and are free to deal outside if terms are not agreed

q: Under dual pricing of inter-divisional transfers, the supplying division is credited at one price and the buying division is charged at a different price. A direct consequence for performance measurement is that:

options.A: The sum of the divisional profits exceeds the profit of the enterprise as a whole, the difference being eliminated on consolidation
options.B: The profit of the enterprise as a whole can never be ascertained
options.C: Both divisions necessarily show a loss on the transfer
options.D: The transfer has no effect on the profit of either division

q: Goal congruence in a divisionalised enterprise means that:

options.A: A manager pursuing the goals set for his own division, as measured by his performance indicators, also acts in the best interests of the enterprise as a whole
options.B: All divisions earn exactly the same rate of return
options.C: Head office takes every operating decision for the divisions
options.D: Divisions are prevented from dealing with one another

q: A divisional manager rejects a sound expansion only because accepting it would dilute the high percentage ROI by which he is judged, even though the expansion earns well above the cost of capital. This behaviour is a recognised dysfunction of:

options.A: Residual Income as a performance measure
options.B: Market-based transfer pricing
options.C: Return on Investment as a performance measure
options.D: Negotiated transfer pricing

q: A proposed project requires an investment of Rs 10,00,000 and is expected to earn a profit of Rs 1,60,000 a year. The cost of capital is 12 per cent. The annual Residual Income expected from the project is:
In a Balanced Scorecard, measures such as the percentage of sales from new products and the customer retention rate are valued chiefly because, unlike the period's profit, they act as:

options.A: Statutory disclosures in the annual accounts
options.B: Purely historical records of past results
options.C: Measures that need no target to be set for them
options.D: Leading indicators that signal future financial performance

q: For a manufacturing division applying the Balanced Scorecard, the measure that fits the internal business process perspective most appropriately is:

options.A: The defect and rework rate in production
options.B: The return on capital employed of the division
options.C: The market share of the division's products
options.D: The hours of training provided per employee

q: For a division applying the Balanced Scorecard, expenditure on upgrading employees' skills and improving its information systems belongs primarily to the:

options.A: Financial perspective
options.B: Customer perspective
options.C: Learning and growth perspective
options.D: Internal business process perspective

options.A: It contains too few financial measures
options.B: It is prepared more than once a year
options.C: It uses non-financial measures at all

q: Non-financial measures of performance are brought into performance evaluation along with financial measures mainly because financial measures alone:

options.A: Report results after the event and reveal little about how the result was achieved or what is being built for the future
options.B: Are expressed in money terms
options.C: Are prepared by the accounts department
options.D: Cannot be compared from one year to another

q: A division compares the working of one of its own functions, such as its stores or payroll function, with the same function in an enterprise in a different industry that performs it exceptionally well. This is an example of:

options.A: Internal benchmarking
options.B: Competitive benchmarking
options.C: Functional benchmarking
options.D: Product benchmarking only

q: In a benchmarking exercise, the step that must come before practices are adapted from the benchmark partner is:

options.A: Publishing the division's own results
options.B: Measuring the performance gap and understanding the practices and conditions that produce the partner's superior performance
options.C: Changing the name of the process studied
options.D: Fixing the next year's budget allotment

options.A: Increase the cost of inspection and of failures by the same amount

options.D: Producing strictly to the minimum specification at the lowest cost

q: A divisional performance report that is to be used for judging the divisional manager should present the result of the division most usefully by:

options.D: Lower than any price charged to an outside customer

options.D: The capital employed in its denominator is low, so the same profit yields a higher percentage return

q: A division has sales of Rs 96,00,000, a profit of Rs 7,20,000 and capital employed of Rs 48,00,000. Its Return on Investment, worked out as profit margin multiplied by capital turnover, is:

options.A: Division B is better, with Rs 3,00,000 against Rs 2,00,000 of Division A

options.A: The profit after all head-office allocations to the total assets of the enterprise

options.C: The sales of the division to its variable costs

q: Under the two-part tariff method of transfer pricing, the buying division is charged:

options.A: Only a single price equal to the market price for every unit

q: Where there is no outside market at all for an intermediate product transferred between divisions, the transfer price is most commonly based on:

options.A: Cost, with or without a mark-up, or on negotiation founded on cost information
options.B: The price of the final product sold to customers
options.C: The price charged for a wholly different product that has a market
options.D: A price fixed by the external auditors of the enterprise

q: A division reports, along with its monthly profit, the number of customer complaints received and the proportion of deliveries made on time. In performance evaluation these two measures are useful chiefly as:

options.A: Substitutes for the profit figure in the annual accounts

q: A divisional manager who expects that a good performance this year will simply be met by a proportionately harder target next year may hold back performance in the current year. This behaviour in target setting is known as the:

options.A: Controllability effect

q: Economic Value Added differs from the Residual Income of a division most essentially in that Economic Value Added:

options.A: Makes no charge at all for the capital employed

q: For a service division applying the Balanced Scorecard, the measure that fits the customer perspective most appropriately is:

options.A: The cost per transaction processed by the division

q: A division adopts, without change, the practices of a benchmark partner operating on a much larger scale and under different conditions, and the expected gains do not materialise. The failure illustrates that benchmarking:

options.A: 7,900 units

q: In a reconciliation of cost and financial accounts which starts with the profit as per the financial accounts, interest on capital charged only in the cost accounts is:

options.A: Deducted from the financial profit, because the cost profit is lower by that amount
options.B: Added to the financial profit, because it is an income of the business
options.C: Ignored, because notional charges never affect a reconciliation
options.D: Shown only as a memorandum note below the reconciliation statement

q: In the operating costing of a road transport undertaking, which of the following is a maintenance charge?

options.A: The annual road licence fee of the vehicle
options.B: The salary of the traffic manager of the undertaking
options.C: The diesel and lubricating oil consumed in running the vehicle
options.D: Repairs, overhauls and servicing of the vehicles

q: In a process, 12,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 4,94,400. Normal loss is 10% of the input and the scrap realises Rs 7 per unit. The cost per unit of the good output is:

options.A: Rs 45
options.C: Rs 48
options.D: Rs 38

q: In contract costing, plant which was issued to a contract site and is returned to the stores before the completion of the contract is dealt with by:

options.A: Crediting the Contract Account with its original cost, ignoring the wear and tear at the site
options.B: Crediting the Contract Account with its written-down value, that is, its value after providing for depreciation for the period it remained at the site
options.C: Debiting the Contract Account again with its full replacement price
options.D: Writing it off entirely to the Costing Profit and Loss Account as a loss

q: The Abnormal Loss Account opened in process costing is finally closed by:

options.A: Crediting the whole value of the abnormal loss to the process account of the next process
options.B: Carrying its balance forward indefinitely as an asset of the factory
options.C: Crediting it with the scrap actually realised on the abnormal loss units and transferring the balance, being the net loss, to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.D: Debiting it with the scrap value of the normal loss of the process

q: Under the constant gross margin method of apportioning joint costs, the share of joint cost borne by a joint product is arrived at by:

options.A: Apportioning the joint cost in the ratio of the weights of the products at the split-off point
options.B: Deducting from the final sales value of the product an amount of gross margin computed at a uniform overall percentage, and then deducting its separable costs after the split-off point
options.C: Charging the joint cost wholly to the product which has the highest final sales value
options.D: Dividing the joint cost equally among all the joint products, whatever their sales values

q: A joint cost of Rs 7,20,000 is to be apportioned among joint products X, Y and Z on the physical units basis. The outputs are: X — 3,000 kg, Y — 2,000 kg and Z — 1,000 kg. The share of joint cost borne by product Y is:
The replacement cost method of accounting for a by-product is applied where the by-product is:

options.A: Used within the factory itself in place of a material that would otherwise have to be purchased, and it is credited to the process at the cost of the material it replaces
options.B: Sold in the open market at the highest price obtainable during the year
options.C: Destroyed immediately after it arises, having no use or value at all
options.D: Further processed into the main product of a subsequent process

q: Under the non-integral (interlocking) system, the account maintained in the financial books to summarise the transactions recorded in the cost ledger is the:

options.A: Work-in-Progress Ledger Control Account
options.B: Stores Ledger Control Account
options.C: Cost Ledger Control Account
options.D: Costing Profit and Loss Account

q: Which of the following items appears in the financial accounts of an enterprise but is not recorded in its cost accounts?

options.A: Wages paid to the direct workers engaged on production
options.B: Interest and dividends received on investments held by the enterprise
options.C: Depreciation charged on the factory plant and machinery
options.D: Cost of the stores consumed in the factory during the period

q: A joint cost of Rs 6,00,000 is to be apportioned between joint products A and B by the net realisable value method. A can be sold for Rs 8,00,000 after further processing costing Rs 2,00,000. B can be sold for Rs 5,00,000 after further processing costing Rs 1,00,000. The share of joint cost borne by product A is:
A recognised difficulty in applying the market value (sales value at split-off) method of apportioning joint costs is that:

options.A: It requires the physical output of each product to be weighed at the split-off point
options.B: It can be used only where all the joint products are sold without any further processing
options.C: It charges no joint cost at all to the product having the lowest sales value
options.D: Market prices at the split-off point may not exist for products which are never sold in that intermediate state

q: In a process, all the material is introduced at the very beginning of the process. The closing work-in-progress of the process will accordingly be taken, for the purpose of equivalent units in respect of material cost, as:

options.A: Nil, because the units are not yet complete
options.B: Complete only to the same extent as it is complete in respect of labour cost
options.C: Fully complete, that is, at 100 per cent of its units
options.D: Complete to one-half of its units in every case

q: A joint product can be sold at the split-off point for Rs 48 per unit. It can alternatively be processed further at an additional cost of Rs 17 per unit and then sold for Rs 72 per unit. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Sell it at the split-off point, because the joint cost has already been incurred on it
options.B: Process it further, because the additional revenue of Rs 24 per unit exceeds the additional cost of Rs 17 per unit by Rs 7 per unit
options.C: Process it further only if the whole of the joint cost apportioned to it is also recovered
options.D: Stop producing the product altogether, since further processing always adds to cost

q: In the operating costing of a staff canteen run by an enterprise, the most appropriate cost unit for expressing the cost of the service is the cost:

options.A: Per meal served by the canteen
options.B: Per kilogram of provisions purchased for the canteen
options.C: Per employee on the rolls of the enterprise
options.D: Per day for which the canteen building remains open
